subject: physics_2
question_text: Obtain an expression for the wave velocity in terms of wavelength (λ) and frequency (n).

mark_split.label: Wave moves λ in one period T

verification.note: The 1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers, so neither check was run. Physics hand-checked: in one time period T the wave advances one wavelength λ, so V = λ/T; with n = 1/T this gives V = nλ. The book derives the same result through V = ω/k = 2πn/(2π/λ) = nλ — both routes agree.

recall_prompt: Say how far the wave moves in one time period, and the expression for wave velocity that follows.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Distance in one period
lines: In one time period T, every particle
completes one full vibration and the wave
moves forward by one wavelength λ.
steps.margin_note: First mark. The physical sentence — one wavelength per period — is the derivation.
steps.why: The whole result rests on one fact: a wave pattern repeats after exactly one wavelength, and one repeat takes exactly one period. Velocity is then just distance over time.
common_mistakes: Quoting V = nλ from memory with no reason — the mark is for λ in time T, not for the final line.
Mixing up T the time period with T the tension from the string formula — here T is time.

recall.must_convey: That the wave travels one wavelength in one time period, so V = λ/T.
accept: distance over time gives lambda by T

steps.memory_tip: One repeat of the pattern = one wavelength, and it takes one period.

steps.label: The expression
lines: Frequency is the number of vibrations in
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Substitute n = 1/T and box V = nλ.
steps.why: Frequency and period are reciprocals — n vibrations fit in one second exactly when each takes 1/n seconds — so λ/T becomes nλ in one substitution.
common_mistakes: Writing V = n/λ or V = λ/n — check with units: (1/s) × m = m/s only for the product nλ.

recall.must_convey: That substituting n = 1/T gives the wave velocity V = nλ.

steps.memory_tip: Velocity = how many waves per second × how long each wave is: n × λ.

insider_note: V = nλ alone is half the answer — the one-wavelength-per-period sentence is what the first mark pays for.
